items.text: Le Rêve does work best visually. The design, décor, theatre space, everything there, it's just breathtaking for every part of the show. The concept sounds beautiful and appealing but when you go watch the performance it doesn't translate very well for me. I was going to say it's for the design and theatre alone. When I went, the stage itself had tons of problems that I didn't see. They had problems during the show. It repeated a lot so I couldn't enjoy the spectacle of certain things. As a story, it isn't entertaining or fun, but for visual design, it's something else. I agree with Misty Y-- that some love Cirque shows and hate this, but it's a totally different debate. This one reaches for certain things in the Cirques, like their flair, their spectacle, and I think that's where the show falls a bit short for me. So I'd probably watch the show for the visual design, but otherwise maybe spend your money elsewhere.

I paid $38 for this used mechanical keyboard. Got exactly $38 worth, no more no less. Space bar and E key are the problems. E key repeats randomly. I got tired of having to read all of my emails to catch a "meeeting." Also it's pretty rare for me to get that kind of double letter so I just ignore it. That's just how they are. When I press space bar I feel it like I'm nudging a tray full of cutlery. Hollow-sounding. That's the space bar clunking every time. Can't hear it during the day. After midnight I hear that. But I just type around it. Messaged seller which switch did it use? Got tired of waiting. Bought it anyway. A week later, it's already on the desk got the answer: brown switches. Comforts are what make me keep it. Every key has a little bump like half way through the keys stroke and then it doesn't go bottom because fingers get feedback that I know it's registered and then just let go. I can type a big email and my wrists are fine and it was impossible with the lappy's flat keys. Should I keep it? Maybe return it. Return shipping would cost quite a lot of money. And I'd have to use the lappy's keys again. That's fine. I'll live with the rattle and all.

Saw the circus-style show, it's great. I'm just knocking a star off from the rating. Not everything is as good as its marketing would have you think. The plot's a difficult and slow story so can miss bits of dialogue. A few songs are very sleepy too or not suited to what's going on. The guys doing stunts are extremely impressive on the water. The girls are very talented, but the girls I think are even more so as they can stay under water for minutes at a time. The stage and theater is circular, so good view from any seat. And the set pieces and lighting really does make for a very memorable show really. Three different entrances to the stage are used all through the show and they really matter a lot for main changes to the story. The stage really looks beautiful, and the show is very visually impressive. I would like to see more of the effects, especially the fire stuff which is not so great. But it's a small nitpick, a show that is very entertaining and visually impressive which I recommend.

People keep selling remote work like some miracle cure. Been mentoring 5 juniors for two years? For jrs who're just learning to code, it's massively overhyped. Jrs usually don't care about tickets and documentation and endless meetings. They need to just be there, join design chats, and see how folks deal with bugs. Need to stop the confusion, be able to ask questions right away. That stuff happens around the water cooler, not on Zoom. It takes way more skill (and it's tough!) knowing when to grab a senior's attention, schedule a sync, or explain an issue you barely get, when not there in person. I've seen the review stuff in remote. A few words on the codebase? For a jr, it sounds like last word instead of help to learn from. Also more lag, less momentum. For all the jrs I've mentored? They grow way faster, much more in person with pairing/whiteboard and free access to seniors. Don't mean to be anti-flexibility. Can be wonderful if you're self-driven. For jrs, proximity can help so much. Confidence, context, instincts, not a laptop and calendar. It slows how well jrs progress. In future that makes less technical leadership and skills in team.

Might not be paranoia to check a lock that is not broken. The mixer is just doing the same thing, same drone. Flour dust in the air, like snow. It's 3:17 AM and Elias was going over to check the front lock. A ritual. Sourdough loaves resting on wooden boards. Crusts still soft, before last bake. So he wiped his hands on his apron, fabric stiff with dough and sweat. And he walks over the front counter. And there it is. The History of Salt, in a hardback, blue spine is cracked near the hinge. And this appears every Thursday for six weeks. Always on the glass display case, beside the unsold cinnamon rolls, exactly. No stamp or library, the bakery is not a municipal branch of the system. When Elias picked it up, the cover was cold. And he opened it. And no empty pages. A folded square of lined paper fell out with a tap. And he opened it. Jagged handwriting. And the note said, you knead with your left hand, dominant. Left hand stop favouring right. And he stared at his red knuckles and the white dusted hands, looked at himself. And the mixer goes through the next cycle. Elias closed the book. Placed it back on the glass and aligned the spine with the edge, turning off the light above the display. And that's the image, leaving the book in the shadows.

Apple has got to stay on this list. At my school we could only have Apple computers. For middle and high school. They were about twice the price of PC machines. And they broke monthly really. Even though I never knocked my laptop anywhere, I swapped the hard drive, reinstalled windows (windows) five times over four years. And an extreme instance, my friends Macbook Pro caught fire for some reason watching a movie while the smoke alarm went off. And apple support really couldn't identify our problems, so they would simply back the computer up, wipe it out and restore the files. And that's the pattern I would say with my own personal experience and with many many friends' experience. Same thing goes for iPhones of course. I had the first one. It was always buggy and malfunctioned frequently. And now a new iPhone comes out, roughly every two months, I mean every few months, maybe a better camera, but it's pretty much the same. Will concede one positive, the iPad's are better than anything we have at the moment as tablets, but Android tablets will catch up.

I’ve been to Las Vegas a ton growing up, watched a ton of Vegas shows before my 21st birthday. So I know these shows, and I know what’s a good show and what’s not.

My take on the Awakening show at Wynn Las Vegas. It’s not bad, but it’s not a must-see Vegas act. It’s just, it’s not a “if I’m going to Vegas anyway I’ll go see this” type of show. It’s not that good.

What’s very good about the show is the stage, the circular stage. Whatever seat you get, you get a decent, pretty good view of the show, which is very unusual for these Vegas shows. Plus, I was able to get it for a good discount. Normally, it’s a $125 ticket for a regular ticket, so it’s $99 if you’re staying in the Wynn or Encore hotel. That’s a good deal. If you’re coming to Vegas anyway, or you’re staying in the Wynn/Encore, and you’ve never been, the $99 is a good deal. That’s good news. The show itself is not that good.

There are some excellent feats, some great acts, but lots of them I’ve seen in Cirque du Soleil type of show, just as well. That’s not bad because in fact it’s good, but the story in the show is very bad. It’s not clear, it’s not well told, it’s not really there at all. At least some of it is not really explained. I don’t know the point of the show. I left not knowing what the show is. A lot of it is happening, not all at once. Too many visuals, too many moving parts, too many gimmicks for an attempt to wow the audience, but it would have been better in my opinion with a few cool stunts and a more restrained approach than to try to wow everyone all the time. So the average of the show was just average. I wasn’t that blown away with it, and it doesn’t seem like the people I went with were very blown away or overwhelmed at all. Some of my friends really liked it, so if you haven’t been, it’s worth seeing it once. Don’t pay full price and then don’t go see the show ever again. It’s too much of this stereotype of Vegas spectacular of just “more is more”. It’s more for the sake of more.

Grabbed this mechanical keyboard second-hand cheapo $38. Its a ride but has been surprisingly decent. Seller was terrible at communication, I messaged them on switch type (before I bought it), they took a week to reply, with a one word answer at which point I had already placed an order on spec. Condition of the board? Well loved. The space bar rattles like a brick (or a loose lego brick, but it's incredibly annoying) and the E key repeats now and then: so i get typos like "theee" rather than "the" lol. But plot twist. I love typeing on it honestly, feedback is excellent tactile, super comfortable for long wanky work mails, I considered returning it, but a slab of plastic for $38? Nah. So I'll tune it. And it's a bargain buy if you mind some DIY, and the double tapping letter, but its good.

Float valves control water fill in the drinking trough. A float is connected to the valve and it moves with the water. When water levels drop the float lowers, opening the valve, letting water in. As water rises, the float goes up and closes it. At the set level it shuts off. Sometimes troughs overflow because crud or mineral buildup stops the valve from closing all the way. Other times the float is adjusted wrong, set way too high so it shuts down after trough is already overflowing.

Water moves from one container to another over a high lip without using a pump — so gravity takes care of it. To start the whole deal, you've got to fill the tube full with water to hold an unbroken column of water. Then with gravity, the length of tube that is going down has a column of water pulling water in over the lip from the source. This low pressure zone is the part that will be at the top of the arch over the arch of the siphon. That's the pressure differential. When water gets down the leg of the siphon, it creates a low pressure zone, and the atmospheric pressure is greater than this low pressure zone, and it forces water up the suction side. The flow stops when the water in the low leg gets close to the water level in the source. The outlet needs to be lower than the source water level. If that is not lower... the driving force for the siphon action needs the difference in water height. So if it's close to the water level or above, then it isn't going to work. And when you have air enter the tube, that breaks the liquid column, and it has to be re-primed by filling it again.

The sourdough sat on its second rise when I spotted the whole affair, again. Always Thursday, always on top of the flour bin, and with my copy of The Count of Monte Cristo left behind. Richmond Public Library stamped. I'm not really too concerned on how they've slipped through the squeaky screen door without me knowing. Frankly, I was in bed, half as aware as could be at 3:00 AM with my whole brain filled with yeast and coffee. And yet this time, something more was present; a piece of yellow legal paper, pokes a tip out of the spine of it like it has been read, like a bookmark. Wipe hands off the apron, leave a white streak on it like a ghost. I pulled the scrap out, it said Page 142, please, I think they're watching the drop box now, that's all. Written in jagged writing, it looked frantic but no real urgency to me as I was on it. I looked toward front door, dark but just my own tired face reflecting back at me, cold draft came in smelling of wet pavement and rain coming on. And I didn't open the book. Just put the note back inside the book, put the book inside the brown bag from the local grocery, and twisted the top of the bag twice so it wouldn't get out.

I spent 38 dollars on a secondhand mechanical keyboard. And i'd say i got around $38 worth out of it, maybe $38.50.
It has issues. The spacebar rattle is bad. Everytime i hit it, it feels really loose. Like a plate of cutlery being pushed around. In daytime it gets lost, but at night its way louder than it should be. The letter E just repeats, so a word like meeting becomes meeeting. Not all the time, but every few paragraphs my finger hit the E, the e gets repeated. Annoying but not the worst.
Communication with the seller was slow. So i asked what switches it has, but i got response only after a week. Which meant it was a waste of keyboard as I got the keyboard before knowing switches. I did not buy the keyboard, but sold the keyboard and it arrived, then i got response, brown switches. Anyway.
The good is it feels nice. The keys are cushioned and they feel nice and i can write long emails and not get wrist pain. That is good and i don't have issues even if i write long emails on my laptop.
Went back? Maybe next time. Didn't want to waste time shipping back to this guy, didn't feel worth it. So on my desk it stays with me. Making noises, E repeat and i'll proofread a lot. Three stars.

Good evening everyone. I'm [Name], and it doesn't seem to matter as I'm the guy Tom roomed in a bunk bed with from like age 3, or until he turned 14. It wasn't always easy, with snoring and fights about the top bunk, but those are just memories. I've been following Tom's life for a long time and saw early on, as kids, how reliable a guy he could be, which we are happy to be celebrating. Tom is a person you can count on, always. Le Reve had a pretty good score. This is a review of Cirque du Soleil. Never wanted to see a show, and this was my first one. But my personal rating, I thought it was a 2.5 or 3 star. The show was very impressive. Was not my style, not the acrobatics, and the interpretive dancing, the theatrically. The way they move, it's not my style. For those who really like theatrical shows, it'll be great for them. For me, I would not spend more than $100. And luckily I got free tickets. And I am very very pleased I did not have to pay money. And not to waste my money.

School attendance logs are a bit boring, but they actually provide a glimpse of what daily life was like that we don't really get from history texts. We learn whether kids were at school or not, and how committed they were to coming to school. What's cool is that from just that you can understand why the kids weren't present. Maybe they just didn't come due to a seasonal change in work. Maybe they had a cold. But this kind of insight is hard to come by. There are gender, age, or social class differences in the information. We learn about how attending school fits with life. If studied for years, this kind of data will show the changing nature of the practice of schooling. It's all a great insight to the development of public health practices and so on, but only so. It's just that only the school recorded whatever they wanted. There wasn't an explanation for the kids' perspective and it's just that they did and didn't, but it's always useful when comparing with other data.

At 2:17 Thursday mornings, Mara always found the field guide to moths on the back steps. The same book every time. It had a county library sticker in the front and a lot of flour dusted on it too. Looks like it’s been in the ovens for years or something. She returned it twice. The library is just being polite about the return. Third week, I don’t care about returning it anymore, I leave it next to my sourdough starter. Nothing more.

Tonight it was raining a lot. Tapping on the back door in the alley and in front door. The ovens were still hot. I was in the middle of butter shaping my croissants, just pushing with both hands against the dough, and the lock just clicks. It’s nothing much just a small click. Nobody’s outside. Just the book, dry in the rain and just sitting on the ground.

So I dry off my hands on my apron and flip the book open. Between “Luna moth” and “Promethea” is a sheet of paper, just folded once. And this is your window. It’s the only lit thing on this street, I come down and I sit by the window and I can read until the first buses arrive. Sorry for the crumbs.

I look over the alley at the damaged milk crates, steam coming out of the drains. And the city feels really big for a second, and then it’s not really. And I rip off a little piece from my order pad and write on it: cinnamon rolls 4:05. I place it in the book and put it on the warm window sill, unlock the back door and wait.

For this class project, we tested how stable different folded cardboard bridges could be. Kids made short beam, arch inspired, and triangular fold bridges from the same cardboard, trying to keep length and width as even as we could. We put each one between two supports and started adding small weights bit by bit. You watch until it bents or tips or collapses.

It's limited - they're handmade, few trials, classroom conditions. So they should not be treated as an engineering data. But overall the triangular fold designs held weight more steady. So fold geometry really does make a difference in stability on model bridges.

Marguerite found the book sitting on the steel table by the back door. Its a Field Guide to Coastal Birds. I don't know if its his or not, she thought. I just like it, that it's there anyway. The Harbor Street library stamp said due March, and we have this system where you should return by March. We'll see. The mail slot is nailed shut years ago, so it can't be by mail, unless somebody just broke in through the mail slot, or through the delivery hatch beside it. That hatch that flour man uses. That hatch doesn't latch up properly.
On 11 Thursdays I asked the day staff. I checked the hatch for scratches, went around 4 once. Left my clothes on to hang at 3 and go home early. Nothing. I wasn't in the room, i was at the ovens with my back to the door. So when its between 2-4. So, this night the receipt was at the oystercatchers with blotchy handwriting where the pen had been held down too hard. I keep meaning to return the book, and every time I pass your door I smell the bread from your ovens and I put it down instead. I can stop if you want. I smelled of salt, she thought, whoever it is that left it. So she made a roll, stuck it in a paper bag and wrote on the back of the receipt bring it Thursday and I'll have a roll.

It's weird seeing people defending Hydro Ottawa lately. I don't use them anymore, I live in Toronto now. I'll tell people about the billing situation since it feels out of whack.
Anyway, I used to use them. Got my account for one year, apartment downtown. I'm not living here, I'm living in with my parents for my MA. I closed my account officially and paid my outstanding charges. And that is a good idea in case it does it, but they never, they keep taking money from my account for another year+ even after I had closed my account. Just random weeks or months, I call customer service, I sent them evidence of the debit happening. They just deny it. Every time it's a new rep, and then it happens again and again.
When my parents and I sat together reviewing our utility bills, we found a mistake. They just linked my banking details with my parents' billing number. My parents mentioned moving in home to them, and it linked my account details to the parents' account. They didn't notice it, it would have been confusing for them with all the money going back to them.
So, it took hours. Multiple phone calls, multiple reps. It was very confusing. But a manager looked into it finally and corrected it. It didn't fix all the refunds. At first, no money back, only an apology. It's a very big problem. I don't give my banking details again in the future. This company is careless with customers' own data. It concerns me deeply, and I believe it should concern every consumer.

It was 3:40, second rye proofing, and there it was. Marisol finds the same book again, on the flour bin by the back door. Fourth Thursday in a row. Same A Field Guide to Night Birds, stamped Eastgate Branch, due 3 weeks ago. Every Thursday she puts it in the dropbox and every Thursday it turns up, and it feels like the building itself is keeping it. She's been carrying it to the drop box on her way home every Thursday, but the book keeps finding it.

Wiped hands on her apron, opens book, a little card flies out from the page on Barn Owls. Rye out at 4:15.

Fan still running. Outside, it smells like bread until 5 am. R walks her mother's dog - poor woman is not able to anymore. She's been forgetting it, or not wanting to return it. She reads it twice. Turns it over, writes with a little grease pencil she uses for marking trays: Rye out at 4:15. Then she tears off a heel from yesterday's loaves and wrap it with wax paper, puts the book on top and pushes the back door open by an inch.

So I did exactly that, was told there was nothing there. What was I to say? £20 gone, very upset! And then the gate agents charged me £5 extra as I had water in the luggage, which was bought inside airport. But now Ryanair don't fly from Liverpool John Lennon to Stockholm Skavsta so I have to fly Norwegian Air. Norwegian customer service is awful to. But on a positive note the flight is newer than Ryanair, not as old looking.

It's a shame. You're not alone, I've got Brandywines just split in the same way. Got a good drenching on Tuesday, by Thursday half of them dropped. You can see it on the fruit. Seam runs right down the side. What happens - no, it's the whole weather situation is a dry spell and then a lot of water. And the inside of the fruit takes water in faster than the skin can stretch, and it splits. So it's a shame. Sungolds I'm finding are holding up better, but I've got a few of them split as well. So it's no use once it's happened but just pick out the ones that are split and put them to use for something else.

But with Brandywines it's a lot more hassle. They've got that thick skin, that's a real problem. And for Sungolds if you can keep them not quite so wet at one go, you may well be okay and they may hold on.

On Thursdays, a book shows up, not just anywhere, I'd say its wedged behind the flour, close to the back door, so whoever puts it there doesn't make me trip. And it's always the same one. Field Guide to North American Moths, Elmwood branch, due date so old that the ink's kind of gone violet. But it's always the same book and I never saw anyone leave it. Every day before 2 pm I'm going down and mixing the rye flour and dough, so I don't pay attention and if a whole marching band walked in during that time, I wouldn't notice. First few weeks it was just placed on the shelf by register and by Friday morning it's gone. Thursdays, same time. OK people are strange. I'm a guy who talks to the flour, so I don't really complain. Tonight there was a note on page 114 that says luna moth. It says, it only live a week and don't eat and I think that's such a waste of a pretty thing. "You get it before it gone?" It's in pencil, no name. Hard pressed. I read it twice, then I read it again when the ovens were doing that ticking sound. I took the first loaf off, wrapped it up in brown paper and put it behind the flour, same spot.

I've stayed inside all day, but the air is just... bad, the air doesn't move around. So even the room is 22 degrees, but it's hot and stuffy because of the humidity. My fan's on and my aircon is on full, but the room still feels stuffy, and you can't open the windows either. So yeah, it feels really stifling just because of the lack of cross air, lack of ventilation. It gets bad after lunchtime. It'll improve once the temp gets high enough that you can open the windows. But it feels pretty suffocating at the moment, very stifling.

You get told remote work is a win for everybody, but it isn't. I've mentored five engineers over the past two years so I can say for my experience it isn't. I see new grads not having the opportunity to see a design argument play out around a whiteboard. Or not seeing a senior engineer get through a nasty bug that the juniors haven't really had a shot at fixing. So they're not getting that transfer of information they would have gotten for free in an office. And then they have to learn when to interrupt someone to ask for help, figure out how to get set up on a phone call, or explain something they may not even understand themselves yet. And that's a very steep task if they haven't really been trained to do it.

And I see where the setup breaks the feedback loop in really interesting ways. A short note on a code review sounds like a judgment on a person. So people just go quiet, they get the message and they stop doing the work. Or they wait for clarification, it's delayed by hours and momentum gets killed. All of those things get really bad if you put all your engineers in separate locations. The five engineers I've worked with have grown so much quicker because they could sit and pair on problems and actually get a senior engineer. It doesn't mean that it's bad if everyone has autonomy, and they know how to direct themselves. But if someone's just started on the job they really need to be around people and get confidence and context and judgment. I do think that we'll end up with weaker technical leadership down the line if we just hand a person a laptop and a calendar to be on their own.

A rain gauge catches rain falling through an opening of known area, and we report this result as a depth. Usually its millimetre or inches, and this depth of water indicates how deep the water would spread over a level surface, were it not drained, evaporated or soaked in. Many gauges are funnels of a wide opening, and they lead into a narrower measuring tube. The small amounts of rain can be read more precisely, since with same volume of water, its height will be greater in the narrower tube. The scale of the tube is marked, considering the ratio of area of funnel opening and the tube, such that the readings would give rainfall depth as required. The wind is a common source of error. Wind around a gauge is going to blow rain around the opening, and therefore, if there is rain, the rain is going to be blown past and hence will under count the true values. Same with evaporation or spilling of rain before reading would skew the outcome.

bought it used for $38. Felt fair. Took it out of the box, bit of dust between keys, some spots on the caps but not too terrible as used. The comfy factor is pretty damn good. write a lot of emails for work and my hands feel more roomy on this than my office flat one and the switches are nice, steady and not so hard. It is solid, not too light and slides on my desk. The space bar is rattly every time you press. Loudly so and it's audible even in quiet mornings. One letter, the e, repeats itself from time to time, if I type faster than usual it'll spell like "neeed" or something similar. Not all time but enough times i notice and proof read more carefully now. I also asked seller on what switches it had got and they answered a week later, which was late since I already got the keyboard. So, for $38, kept it. The shipping cost would be more than $38 and more hassle than it's worth.

The neighborhood repair café needs you bringing in one broken item, per person. Check in at the front table and take a numbered ticket which you must keep until it is done. You will be called in order by the volunteers. They might need some input on fixing it and it isn't easy. So if you're able to hang around, do that, so that if I need any decisions or any input, please do be nearby. We cannot fix everything in here, so parts need to be ordered. You pick up your item before the volunteers leave, which is 4:30 p.m., and unclaimed items can't be kept here.

Went to this buffet on a Friday at 4:30pm. There wasn’t really a line at all. Paid ~130 USD for two, felt a bit high. Before we went in I was assuming it would be on par with a steak house, and it actually was more. It wasn’t even as good and the food wasn’t amazing. I feel like you could spend less money at other Las Vegas buffets and get lamb, prime rib, chicken etc. It was disappointing there’s no steak. For this price I expected some kind of steak, and even a good beef burger would have been great.
The seafood section is interesting. There were Alaska crab legs (also available in many other Vegas buffets) and rock crab claws which I have not seen in other buffets. The main issue was no crab mallets, and they said they do have wooden mallets but our table was close to another and I didn’t want to break shells and send pieces at them. I only ate the legs. I think there were some mallets at the buffet but I couldn’t spot them, I’ll look for it more, and maybe I just didn’t notice, and it was just there.
The asian section wasn’t really any different, it seemed just like the buffet at Rampart casino. Dessert had gelato and pastries, but nothing special. Had fresh juice, but we didn’t try it.
It’s acceptable, but overpriced, and if there is no wait I’d try it at some point just to see what it’s like. If its a wait, I might not.

Old school attendance logs give us a good lens back into how people used to live. Historians use them to get the daily rhythms of a community, and it works surprisingly well. The records will show you patterns of attendance that are being driven by seasons, so planting, harvest, harsh weather, and also outbreaks of disease, flu in particular. If the rates of school attendance suddenly plummets, what it's indicating is a local outbreak of flu, or the community might need their kids in the harvest, so education is competing with economic need. And if certain groups of kids are not attending class, that can reflect underlying social inequalities and what the culture felt was important and what it wasn't. There are caveats though, and we have to go and check these numbers against other information and do our detective work. It is possible for a teacher or headmaster to tamper with their figures to match expectations and get through funding and scrutiny from the education department. And most registers won't even tell you why a student was not there.

The float valve is how the trough stays filled. A pressurized water line goes to it and its float ball or block, which is attached to a lever arm to a plunger, washer etc. So when cows drink and the level drops, this ball will sink and it pulls the plunger off of its seal and then water starts flowing into the trough. Then it starts to rise, ball goes up on the lever and pushes that plunger back to the washer, gradually decreasing it until its off. And its very common with the washer wearing out or getting clogged, that's the main reason why it's always running all the time. The other, the washer is good but the float gets poked, gets water logged, and it just doesn't rise. So the plunger doesn't get pushed back against the seat or the washer and it overflows.
